outcome: Bedert, Draganić, Müyesser and Pavez-Signé (arXiv:2603.08675, March 2026) prove the Lovász conjecture for Cayley graphs of degree d > n^{1-c}. This settles a restricted class of the conjecture. [Judged 2026-09-28; the researcher's original outcome follows.] The conjecture (every connected vertex-transitive graph has a Hamiltonian path, and the stronger Thomassen version that sufficiently large ones have a Hamiltonian cycle) remains open, but the lower bound on the longest cycle/path guaranteed in an n-vertex connected vertex-transitive graph was improved twice in the window: from the prior Ω(n^{3/5}) to Ω(n^{13/21}) (Groenland, Longbrake, Steiner, Turcotte, Yepremyan, Aug 2024), then to Ω(n^{9/14}) (Norin, Steiner, Thomassé, Wollan, May 2025), then to n^{2/3-o(1)} (Bucić, Christoph, Pokrovskiy, Steiner, Jun 2026). A separate 2026 paper proved the conjecture for a restricted dense-Cayley-graph regime. A July 2024 preprint by Misa Nakanishi claims a full proof for the special case of odd order, but it is unread by experts and its version history (43KB collapsing to 3KB over two revisions within a month) is a red flag; it is treated as an unverified claim, not a verified partial result.

disputes.summary: Misa Nakanishi's arXiv:2407.00646 claims a proof that every connected vertex-transitive graph with an odd number of vertices is Hamiltonian (a case of the conjecture). The paper is unread/undigested by the expert community as far as could be established, and its own revision history is suspicious: v1 (30 Jun 2024) was 43KB, v2 (10 Jul 2024) and v3 (30 Jul 2024) each shrank to 3KB, suggesting the original argument was retracted or drastically cut rather than merely polished. No survey, blog, or citing paper found treats this as an accepted result; the Wikipedia article and subsequent papers on the conjecture (e.g. arXiv:2408.04618, arXiv:2505.08634, arXiv:2606.09742) do not cite or build on it. Because it is unverified, it is not used as the basis for `status` and is recorded here rather than as `partial`.

summary: The frozen-revision statement is the Lovász conjecture that every connected vertex-transitive graph contains a Hamiltonian path (with the Thomassen strengthening that sufficiently large such graphs are Hamiltonian). Both remain open. What happened in the window is a sequence of genuine bound improvements on the longest guaranteed cycle/path length in an n-vertex connected vertex-transitive graph, each explicitly framed by its authors as progress toward Lovász's conjecture, not a resolution: Groenland, Longbrake, Steiner, Turcotte and Yepremyan (arXiv:2408.04618, submitted 8 Aug 2024, revised Oct 2025) improved the bound from Ω(n^{3/5}) to Ω(n^{13/21}); Norin, Steiner, Thomassé and Wollan (arXiv:2505.08634, submitted 13 May 2025) improved it further to Ω(n^{9/14}); and Bucić, Christoph, Pokrovskiy and Steiner (arXiv:2606.09742, submitted 8 Jun 2026, revised 24 Jul 2026) improved it again to n^{2/3-o(1)} using sublinear-expander techniques. Separately, Bedert, Draganić, Müyesser and Pavez-Signé (arXiv:2603.08675, v2 dated 20 Apr 2026) proved the conjecture outright for a restricted regime — Cayley graphs of degree d > n^{1-c} for a small constant c — which is a genuine case of the conjecture (a restriction on the class of graphs), though the bulk of the literature and the general conjecture remain open. I read the full text or acknowledgements of each of these four papers and found no mention of AI, machine learning, or large-language-model assistance in any of them; the one acknowledgement present (in arXiv:2603.08675) thanks a human colleague for a bibliographic pointer. I also chased a spurious lead: one WebFetch pass on arXiv:2606.09742 claimed a 'Statement of AI use' subsection existed in Section 4, but three independent re-fetches (the ar5iv mirror read in full, a heading-by-heading listing of v1, and a fetch aimed squarely at that subsection) found no such section anywhere in the paper, so I treat that claim as a hallucination of the fetch tool's summarizer rather than a real finding — it does not appear in the record. Separately, arXiv:2407.00646 (Misa Nakanishi, first posted 30 Jun 2024) claims a full proof of the odd-order case, but it shows no sign of expert digestion or citation by the later papers above, and its own version history (43KB draft collapsing to 3KB across two rapid within-month revisions) is a strong signal of a withdrawn or badly broken argument rather than mere polish; I did not find any explicit retraction notice, so I record it as an unread claim/dispute rather than either a verified partial result or a confirmed error. I also verified that a related-sounding paper, arXiv:2505.05339 ('A Counterexample to a Conjecture of Lovász'), concerns an entirely different 1975 Lovász conjecture on hypergraph matching numbers (refuted via the Biggs–Smith graph's line hypergraph) and is out of scope — a case where the triage's own found item needed disambiguation, which it had already flagged as unread. On balance, `status` is `progress`: the conjecture itself is untouched, but the quantitative bound that measures how close current techniques come to it moved substantially three times in the window, and one restricted case was fully settled. No AI system was found to be involved in any of this work.
competing_reading: The Bedert–Draganić–Müyesser–Pavez-Signé result (moderately dense Cayley graphs) could arguably be classified as `partial` rather than folded into a `progress` status, since it is a genuine case of the conjecture (a restriction to a subclass with a density condition) that was fully settled, not merely a bound improvement. I chose `progress` as the overall status because the Wikipedia bullet is about the general conjecture and the dominant, most-discussed activity in the window is the sequence of asymptotic bound improvements (which by §3.1 do not equal a resolved case, since existence of a long cycle is not the same kind of statement as Hamiltonicity of a subclass); a case could be made for reporting the Cayley-graph paper's event as the anchor instead, with resolution_direction `confirmed`. Likewise, if Nakanishi's odd-order claim were ever independently verified, the correct status would become `partial` with `resolution_direction` `confirmed` for that case.
what_would_settle_it: An expert citation, digestion, or explicit erratum regarding arXiv:2407.00646 would resolve whether Nakanishi's odd-order claim is correct, withdrawn, or simply ignored. A survey or Wikipedia-article update explicitly crediting the Bedert et al. Cayley-graph result as 'a case of the Lovász conjecture now settled' versus 'progress toward it' would settle the partial-vs-progress classification.
